analysis.one_liner: Taxes fortunes above $1 billion to fund rebates, Medicare dental and vision, child care, and $60k teacher pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2026 with 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, and sent to four House committees; none has taken it up, and no vote has occurred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 5% annual tax on the net wealth of any household with more than $1 billion in assets, and use the money for a package of programs aimed at ordinary families: $3,000-per-person rebates, Medicare coverage of dental, hearing, and vision care, an $85.6-billion-a-year housing fund, a new child care entitlement for children under six, a $60,000 minimum salary for public school teachers, and permanent protections for people receiving home care. It would also repeal the health care cuts in the 2025 reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21) and let people above 400% of the poverty line qualify for premium tax credits. As of now it has only been introduced and referred to committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under six earning up to 250% of their state's median income get guaranteed child care assistance; Medicare beneficiaries gain dental, hearing aid, and eyeglass coverage; every public school teacher gets a $60,000 salary floor; households receive $3,000 ($6,000 for couples) plus $3,000 per dependent in 2026 rebates; ACA enrollees above 400% of poverty regain premium credits; people with disabilities get expanded home and community-based care; renters benefit from a Housing Trust Fund funded at $85.6 billion a year. All paid for by an annual 5% tax on household fortunes over $1 billion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families, seniors, teachers, and disabled people

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 5% annual tax on the net value of assets held by anyone whose wealth exceeds $1 billion (married couples counted as one taxpayer, threshold inflation-adjusted), backed by an ownership registry, new information reporting, a requirement that the IRS audit at least 50% of these taxpayers each year, and enforcement funding equal to 1% of the tax's revenue.
Provides 2026 'affordability rebates' of $3,000 per adult ($6,000 per couple) plus $3,000 per dependent, using the structure of the 2021 stimulus checks.

Repeals the health provisions of Public Law 119-21 (the 2025 reconciliation law), preserving its rural health transformation funds, and removes the 400%-of-poverty-line cap on ACA premium tax credits so premiums are capped at 8.5% of income at every income level.

Adds dental and oral health, hearing aids and audiology, and routine eye exams and eyeglasses to traditional Medicare, with services phased in from 2027 (dentures) and 2028, a 10% payment bonus for dentists in shortage areas, and a phase-in shielding Part B premiums from the cost of dental coverage through 2031.
Authorizes $85.647 billion per year for the federal Housing Trust Fund for fiscal years 2026 through 2035 to build and preserve affordable housing.

Creates a birth-through-five child care and early learning entitlement: every eligible child under age 6 in a family up to 250% of state median income (plus vulnerable children such as those with disabilities, in foster care, or experiencing homelessness) is entitled to care, with payment rates states must set to cover providers' full costs including wages, plus $20 billion in grants to localities and Head Start.
Establishes a $60,000-a-year minimum salary for every public school teacher in the United States, with collective bargaining rules.

Makes permanent the Medicaid protections against spousal impoverishment for people receiving home and community-based services and the Money Follows the Person demonstration, and funds home-care improvement planning and quality grants.

analysis.who_pays: Households and trusts with net assets above $1 billion would owe 5% of their net wealth every year, would be barred from deducting the wealth tax from their income taxes, and would owe 60% on covered assets if they expatriate to avoid it. Dentists, audiologists, and hearing aid and eyeglass suppliers would accept new Medicare fee schedules set at 70% of national median private fees and, for hearing aids and glasses, price caps tied to federal supply schedules and competitive bidding. The Treasury bears the cost of the spending programs, which the bill intends to cover with the wealth tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households with over $1 billion in assets

drawbacks.text: Taxing wealth is harder to enforce than taxing income, especially for stakes in private companies. The bill lets owners of hard-to-value assets elect an estimated value based on average appreciation for their asset class, but only in alternate years, and leaves the detailed valuation rules to the Treasury Secretary; how much money the tax actually raises depends on rules and audits that do not yet exist.

The bill itself includes anti-avoidance machinery — aggregation rules for related trusts, treatment of grantor trusts and incomplete gifts as the owner's own property, children's assets counted against the parent, and a 60% rate on covered expatriates — which is an acknowledgment that wealthy households would otherwise restructure or move assets to escape the tax.

Medicare's new dental fee schedule is set at 70% of the national median private dental fee (with Medicare paying 80% of that), which could make many dentists reluctant to participate and leave seniors struggling to find care, particularly outside shortage areas.

The spending side is enormous and partly open-ended: the Housing Trust Fund is authorized at $85.6 billion a year for a decade and the child care entitlement is appropriated at 'such sums as may be necessary'. No revenue estimate appears in the record, so whether the 5% billionaire tax covers the cost is untested, and if it falls short the gap becomes a general-budget cost.

The bill text provided does not show how the $60,000 teacher salary floor would be funded or how it interacts with state and local pay systems beyond collective bargaining rules, leaving a major fiscal and practical question unanswered in the material available.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the tax collects as written, the cost falls almost entirely on a very small number of billionaire households — about 5% of their net worth each year — while the benefits (child care, Medicare dental and hearing coverage, teacher pay, rebates, home care) reach tens of millions of ordinary families. That is an unusually direct trade. The honest caveats are on execution: wealth valuation and avoidance could erode the revenue, the dental fee schedule may limit how many dentists participate, and the open-ended child care and housing appropriations could outgrow the tax. On paper the benefits are broad and the burden concentrated; in practice everything depends on enforcement the bill delegates to future rulemaking.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the House in March 2026 and referred to four committees, it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote as the 2026 session continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on March 3, 2026.

It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee — the committee that handles taxes — and in addition to Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Education and Workforce, meaning any one of them can hold it.
Seven Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors; no Republican has.
The action history shows nothing after the referral: no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action, and no vote scheduled as of the record provided.
The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but has no movement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained: billionaires owe nothing new, and families, seniors, and teachers the bill targets have received nothing. The practical winners of the current stalemate are billionaire households and the House majority, which avoids a recorded vote on taxing great wealth while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Billionaires and the House majority, so far

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its billionaire wealth tax package in the House.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Republican-controlled)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill's core tax provisions on referral and has taken no action — no hearing or markup — since March 2026.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Leads the committee where the bill's tax provisions sit; the committee has not scheduled it for consideration.

against.name: Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Education and Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Hold the bill's health care, housing finance, and teacher pay provisions; none has acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever occurred, so the parties' positions are untested on the floor; the only evidence is that the sponsor and all 7 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: The bill would take 5% of their net wealth every year, bar them from deducting it against income taxes, count assets parked in trusts and children's names, and charge 60% if they renounce citizenship to escape it. Their interest in keeping the tax from advancing runs directly against the programs it funds.

Restoring ACA premium credits and repealing the 2025 reconciliation law's health provisions keeps subsidized coverage flowing through private insurance plans, adding customers above the 400%-of-poverty line. Insurers and enrollees both gain here.

They would gain a large new pool of Medicare-covered patients from 2027-2028, but at fee schedule rates set at 70% of national median private fees, well below what they charge now; a 10% bonus applies in shortage areas.
Medicare would start paying for hearing aids and eyeglasses for millions of seniors, but prices would be capped at federal supply schedule rates and subject to competitive bidding, squeezing margins.
The new entitlement requires states to set payment rates sufficient to cover providers' full costs, including staff wages, creating a guaranteed public revenue stream for the industry.

Repealing the 2025 reconciliation law's health provisions and restoring premium credits would reduce coverage losses that hit hospital budgets, and rural providers get payment bonuses and preserved rural health funds.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority, no Republican cosponsors, and the bill parked across four committees with no markup scheduled, the realistic path is no further action before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Bills like this — sweeping tax-and-spend packages from the minority party — almost never reach the floor; its more likely function is as a statement of priorities for future campaigns than as a law in this Congress.
